title: Book of Judges IQ
subtitle: Deborah, Gideon, Samson and more. How well do you know the judges?

questions.text: What was the role of a judge in the book of Judges?

options.text: A king who ruled from a throne
options.explanation: Israel had no king yet in this period. The judges were raised up to lead and deliver, not to reign as kings.

options.text: A leader God raised up to rescue Israel from their enemies
options.explanation: Throughout the book, God raises up judges to deliver His people when they cry out for help.
Priests had their own role. The judges were deliverers and leaders rather than priests.

options.text: A scribe who copied the law
options.explanation: The judges were not copyists. They led Israel in times of trouble.

questions.text: Which judge was a woman who also served as a prophetess?

options.explanation: Judges 4 introduces Deborah as a prophetess who judged Israel and went into battle alongside Barak.
Delilah was the woman who betrayed Samson. She was not a judge of Israel.
Jael bravely struck down the enemy commander Sisera, but she was not a judge herself.
Ruth has her own book and story. She does not appear as a judge.

questions.text: How did Gideon test whether God was really calling him?

options.text: He climbed a mountain to look for a sign
options.explanation: Gideon stayed near home for his test. He used a fleece of wool, not a mountain.

options.text: He laid out a fleece of wool and watched for dew
options.explanation: Judges 6 tells how Gideon asked for dew on the fleece but not the ground, then the reverse, to be sure of God's call.
The well known sign Gideon asked for was the fleece and the dew, not casting lots.
There is no forty day fast here. Gideon's test was the fleece.

questions.text: God told Gideon his army was too large. How many men did Gideon keep for the battle?

options.explanation: The final number was far smaller, chosen so the victory would clearly be God's work.
Judges 7 says God reduced Gideon's army to three hundred men so Israel could not boast in its own strength.
Ten thousand remained at one stage, but God trimmed the number further down to three hundred.
The number was three hundred, not one hundred.

questions.text: What unusual weapons did Gideon's small band carry into battle?

options.text: Trumpets and torches hidden in pitchers
options.explanation: Judges 7 describes the men holding trumpets and torches inside empty pitchers, then breaking them to startle the enemy camp.
The surprise of the attack came from trumpets and torches, not ordinary weapons.
Smooth stones belong to David and Goliath. Gideon's men used trumpets and torches in jars.
There were no flaming arrows here. The weapons were trumpets and torches hidden in pitchers.

questions.text: Which judge made a rash vow that brought great sorrow to his own family?

options.explanation: Othniel was the first judge and delivered Israel, but the rash vow belongs to Jephthah.
Judges 11 records Jephthah's vow before battle, which led to deep grief when his daughter met him on his return.
Ehud was the left handed judge who defeated Eglon. The tragic vow was Jephthah's.
Samson had his own troubles, but the rash vow about his family was made by Jephthah.

questions.text: Samson was set apart from birth as a Nazirite. What was a key sign of that vow?

options.text: He could never speak in public
options.explanation: Speaking was never forbidden. A central sign of his vow was his uncut hair.

options.text: His hair was never to be cut
options.explanation: Judges 13 says no razor was to come on his head, for he would be a Nazirite to God from birth.

options.text: He had to wear a golden crown
options.explanation: There was no crown. The visible sign of Samson's vow was his uncut hair.

options.text: He could never leave his hometown
options.explanation: Samson traveled often. The mark of his vow was his hair, not staying home.

questions.text: Who coaxed the secret of Samson's strength out of him?

options.explanation: Deborah was a faithful judge of Israel, not the woman who betrayed Samson.
Judges 16 tells how Delilah pressed Samson until he revealed that his strength was tied to his hair.
Jael acted against the enemy commander Sisera in a different account, not against Samson.
Rahab helped the spies in the book of Joshua. She has no part in Samson's story.

questions.text: How did Samson finally defeat the Philistines at the end of his life?

options.text: He led an army against their city
options.explanation: Samson acted alone at the end. His final victory came in their temple, not on a battlefield.

options.text: He pushed down the pillars of their temple
options.explanation: Judges 16 describes Samson, his strength returned, pushing apart the temple pillars so the building fell on the crowd.
There is no poisoning in the account. He brought down the temple by its pillars.

options.text: He set fire to their fields
options.explanation: Samson did once send foxes through their fields, but his final act was pulling down the temple.

questions.text: Which judge was known for being left-handed and slipped a hidden message to a king?

options.explanation: Gideon is known for the fleece and the three hundred men, not for being left handed.
Judges 3 describes Ehud, a left handed man, who told King Eglon he had a secret message and then delivered Israel.
Barak fought alongside Deborah. The left handed judge with the secret message was Ehud.
Samson was famous for his strength, not for being left handed.

questions.text: What sad cycle keeps repeating throughout the book of Judges?

options.text: The people sin, suffer, cry out, and God sends a deliverer
options.explanation: The book turns again and again on this cycle of falling away, oppression, crying out, and rescue through a judge.

options.text: Kings rise and fall one after another
options.explanation: Israel had no king during this time. The cycle was about sin, suffering, and deliverance.

options.text: The temple is built and torn down repeatedly
options.explanation: The temple was not yet built. The repeating pattern is the cycle of sin and rescue.

options.text: Prophets are sent and ignored each generation
options.explanation: The recurring theme is the cycle of falling into sin and being delivered by a judge, not a string of ignored prophets.

questions.text: How does the book of Judges often describe the spiritual condition of Israel?

options.text: Everyone did that which was right in his own eyes
options.explanation: Judges 21:25 (ASV) reads, "In those days there was no king in Israel: every man did that which was right in his own eyes."

options.text: The people walked faithfully all their days
options.explanation: The book paints a far harder picture, with the people drifting from God again and again.

options.text: Israel was ruled by a wise and godly king
options.explanation: There was no king in this era. The book even notes that fact.

options.text: The whole nation kept the law without fail
options.explanation: Far from it. The book repeatedly shows the people doing what was right in their own eyes.

gradeBands.label: Just Beginning
gradeBands.message: The judges are full of bold stories. Dive in.

gradeBands.label: Coming Along
gradeBands.message: You know some of the judges. A reread will round it out.

gradeBands.label: Well Versed
gradeBands.message: You know the judges and their stories well.

gradeBands.label: Judges Expert
gradeBands.message: Outstanding. You really know this part of the story.
